recipes.title: Spaghetti alla Carbonara
recipes.description: Spaghetti alla Carbonara from Rome, Lazio. A boiled & tossed off the heat preparation built on spaghetti, guanciale, egg yolks, whole egg, pecorino romano.

items.name: Pecorino Romano
items.note: finely grated, plus extra to serve

steps.text: Fry the guanciale in a dry cold pan over medium heat until the fat renders and the pieces are golden and crisp. Take off the heat and keep the fat in the pan.
Whisk the yolks, whole egg, Pecorino and a lot of black pepper into a thick paste.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the spaghetti. Cook until al dente, about 1 minute less than the packet. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Drop the drained pasta into the guanciale pan (off the heat) and toss for 30 seconds so it stops steaming.
Pour in the egg mixture and toss hard, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is glossy and coats every strand. It must not scramble.
Serve at once with more Pecorino and pepper.

recipes.storage: Best eaten immediately. Refrigerate leftovers up to 1 day.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable for freezing — the egg sauce splits on thawing.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a pan with a splash of water, tossing constantly.
chefTips: The pan must be off the heat when the egg goes in — residual warmth is enough to thicken it.
Yolk-heavy custard plus starchy pasta water is what makes it creamy. There is no cream in carbonara.
variations: Use a mix of Pecorino and Parmigiano for a rounder, less sharp finish.
Pancetta is a common substitute for guanciale outside Lazio.
commonMistakes: Adding the egg over direct heat — it turns to scrambled egg.
Draining the pasta bone dry, leaving nothing to loosen the sauce.

recipes.title: Bucatini all'Amatriciana
recipes.description: Bucatini all'Amatriciana from Amatrice, Lazio. A simmered tomato preparation built on bucatini, guanciale, peeled san marzano tomatoes, pecorino romano, dried chilli flakes, dry white wine.

steps.text: Render the guanciale in a dry pan until crisp. Add the chilli and cook 30 seconds.
Pour in the wine and let it evaporate.
Add the tomatoes, season lightly and simmer 15–20 minutes until glossy and thick.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the bucatini. Cook al dente — bucatini stays chewy, so taste often. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through the sauce with a little pasta water, then finish off the heat with most of the Pecorino.
Serve with the remaining Pecorino.

recipes.storage: The sauce keeps 3 days refrigerated; dress fresh pasta to serve.
recipes.freezing: Freeze the sauce (without pasta) up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm the sauce gently, then toss with freshly cooked pasta.
chefTips: Amatrice purists keep the guanciale pieces large so you get crisp bites throughout.
Don't drown it in tomato — it should be a coating, not a stew.
variations: Bucatini is the Roman choice; Amatrice traditionally uses spaghetti.
Some cooks add a little grated onion; classic Amatrice does not.
commonMistakes: Using too much tomato and too little guanciale.
Skipping the rest off the heat before the cheese.

recipes.title: Rigatoni con la Pajata
recipes.description: Rigatoni con la Pajata from Rome, Lazio. A roman offal ragù preparation built on rigatoni, pajata (milk-fed veal small intestine), onion, dry white wine, crushed tomatoes.

items.name: pajata (milk-fed veal small intestine)
items.note: cleaned, tied into rings — from a specialist butcher

steps.text: Have the butcher clean the pajata and help you tie it into small rings; the milk inside sets into a natural creamy sauce as it cooks.
Sweat the soffritto in the oil. Add the pajata rings and colour gently.
Add the wine and reduce, then the tomatoes, clove and chilli.
Braise very gently 1.5–2 hours until the pajata is tender and the sauce is rich and slightly creamy.
Cook the rigatoni, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the sauce with a little pasta water and serve with plenty of Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: This is a traditional 'quinto quarto' Roman dish — buy pajata from a trusted butcher who will prepare it for you.
Low and slow; the sauce should turn faintly creamy from the milk in the pajata.
variations: If pajata is unavailable, the same soffritto-wine-tomato base makes a fine coda alla vaccinara-style oxtail ragù.
commonMistakes: Cooking it fast, leaving the offal tough.
Skimping on the Pecorino.

recipes.title: Tonnarelli Cacio e Pepe
recipes.description: Tonnarelli Cacio e Pepe from Rome, Lazio. A boiled & emulsified preparation built on tonnarelli, pecorino romano, black peppercorns.

items.name: Salt
items.note: for the pasta water — go easy, Pecorino is salty

steps.text: Toast the cracked pepper in a wide dry pan over medium heat for 30 seconds until fragrant, then take off the heat.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the tonnarelli. Fresh tonnarelli need only 2–3 minutes. Cook in less water than usual so it turns very starchy; reserve 2 mugs.
Add a ladle of hot pasta water to the pepper pan and swirl.
In a bowl, work the Pecorino with a little cool pasta water into a smooth, spreadable cream (cool water stops it clumping).
Drain the pasta, add it to the pepper pan with a little more water and toss, then take off the heat and stir through the Pecorino cream, tossing hard until silky.
Loosen with pasta water as needed and serve immediately.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; the sauce stiffens as it cools.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable for freezing.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with plenty of added water, tossing over low heat.
chefTips: Make the cheese into a paste with cool water first — hitting hot grated Pecorino with boiling water is how you get a rubbery lump.
Tonnarelli or spaghetti hold the emulsion best.
variations: Add a knob of butter for a more forgiving, rounder sauce (common in restaurants, less traditional).
commonMistakes: Tossing grated cheese straight into a very hot pan — it seizes.
Not saving enough pasta water.

recipes.title: Fettuccine alla Romana
recipes.description: Fettuccine alla Romana from Rome, Lazio. A braised meat ragù preparation built on minced beef and a little chicken liver, onion, garlic cloves, carrot, red wine, crushed tomatoes, bay leaf.

items.name: minced beef and a little chicken liver

steps.text: Brown the minced beef and a little chicken liver in the oil in batches until well coloured; set aside.
Soften the onion, garlic and carrot in the same pot for 8 minutes.
Return the meat, add the wine and reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes and bay leaf, season, and braise on low heat 1.5–2 hours until the meat is meltingly tender and the sauce is thick.
Cook the fettuccine in well-salted water; reserve a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with grated Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock or water.
chefTips: Brown the minced beef and a little chicken liver properly — colour is flavour in a braised ragù.
Keep the heat low and give it time; the meat should shred, not chew.
variations: A strip of orange or lemon peel in the braise lifts gamey meats.
Swap the fresh ribbons for a sturdy tube if that is the local shape.
commonMistakes: Crowding the pan when browning, so the meat steams grey.
Rushing the braise.

recipes.title: Gnocchi alla Romana
recipes.description: Gnocchi alla Romana from Rome, Lazio. A filled pasta crescents in butter preparation built on rye flour, plain flour, eggs, oil.

steps.text: Knead the dough smooth and rest 30 minutes wrapped.
Mix the filling and season well.
Roll the dough very thin. Cut discs, pipe in a little filling, fold into half-moons and seal firmly.
Cook in gently boiling salted water 3–4 minutes until they float and the seams are tender.
Toss in melted butter with chives and serve with grated Grana.

recipes.freezing: Freeze uncooked on a tray up to 1 month; cook from frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in butter.
chefTips: Squeeze the spinach bone dry — wet filling bursts the parcels.
Seal the edges properly and keep the water at a gentle boil.
variations: Sauerkraut or potato fillings in other Tyrolean valleys.
A pinch of the rye can be swapped for wholemeal.
commonMistakes: Wet filling.
Rolling the dough too thick.

recipes.title: Mezze Maniche alla Gricia
recipes.description: Mezze Maniche alla Gricia from Rome, Lazio. A boiled & emulsified preparation built on mezze maniche, guanciale, pecorino romano.

steps.text: Render the guanciale in a dry pan over medium heat until golden and crisp; keep the fat.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the mezze maniche. Cook al dente with a firm edge. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the drained pasta in the guanciale and its fat over low heat, adding pasta water to make a light sauce.
Off the heat, shower in the Pecorino and plenty of pepper, tossing hard until it emulsifies and clings.
Serve with extra Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Not recommended.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a pan with a splash of water.
chefTips: Gricia is 'carbonara without egg, amatriciana without tomato' — the emulsion is everything.
Low heat when the cheese goes in.
variations: A little white wine deglazed into the guanciale adds depth.
commonMistakes: Burning the guanciale — it turns bitter.
Cheese into too-hot a pan.

recipes.title: Spaghetti alla Carrettiera
recipes.description: Spaghetti alla Carrettiera from Lazio. A raw, storecupboard sauce preparation built on spaghetti, garlic cloves, extra-virgin olive oil, chilli flakes, dried porcini, large handful parsley.

steps.text: Stir the garlic, chilli, parsley and (soaked, chopped) porcini into the oil in a large bowl with a little salt.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the spaghetti. Cook until al dente, about 1 minute less than the packet. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the hot drained pasta straight into the bowl with a splash of pasta water.
Add the Pecorino and toss until it forms a light sauce with the oil and water.
Serve immediately.

recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: A 'carter's' sauce — no cooking, built from what keeps in the pantry.
The heat of the pasta is what 'cooks' the garlic; grate it fine so it mellows.
variations: Sicilian carrettiera adds fresh tomato and basil.
Tuna and a squeeze of lemon make a heartier bowl.
commonMistakes: Chunky raw garlic that stays harsh.
Not enough pasta water to bind.

recipes.title: Pasta alla Zozzona
recipes.description: Pasta alla Zozzona from Rome, Lazio. A boiled, then tossed with a rich pan sauce preparation built on rigatoni, guanciale, italian sausage, cherry tomatoes, egg yolks, pecorino romano, dry white wine.
recipes.method: Boiled, then tossed with a rich pan sauce

steps.text: Render the guanciale in a dry pan until crisp; add the crumbled sausage and brown well.
Add the wine and let it evaporate, then the tomatoes and cook 10 minutes to a thick sauce.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the rigatoni. Cook al dente — the ridges must hold the sauce. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Whisk the yolks with the Pecorino and plenty of pepper.
Toss the drained pasta into the pan (off the heat) with a splash of pasta water, then stir through the yolk mixture, tossing hard until creamy — it must not scramble.
Serve at once with more Pecorino.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; refrigerate up to 1 day.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable — the egg splits.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: Zozzona means 'dirty/messy' — it piles the Roman greatest hits (carbonara, amatriciana, gricia) into one pan.
Add the egg off the heat, exactly as for carbonara.
variations: Some cooks leave the tomato out for a whiter, richer plate.
commonMistakes: Scrambling the egg over heat.
Under-browning the sausage.

recipes.title: Fettuccine con Rigaglie di Pollo
recipes.description: Fettuccine con Rigaglie di Pollo from Rome, Lazio. A slow poultry ragù preparation built on chicken thighs and chicken livers/giblets, onion, garlic cloves, red wine, crushed tomatoes.

items.name: sprig rosemary and a bay leaf

steps.text: Brown the chicken thighs and chicken livers/giblets well in the oil, skin-side first, rendering the fat; set aside and pour off most of the fat.
Soften the soffritto and garlic in the pan 10 minutes.
Return the chicken thighs and chicken livers/giblets, add the wine and reduce, then the tomatoes and herbs. Braise gently 2 hours until the meat falls from the bone.
Lift out the bones, shred the meat and return it; reduce to a thick ragù. Season.
Cook the fettuccine and toss through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with Parmigiano.

recipes.storage: Better the next day; keeps 4 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock.
chefTips: Render the chicken thighs and chicken livers/giblets skin properly — that fat carries the flavour of the whole sauce.
Skim excess fat before serving; poultry ragù can be rich.
variations: Goose ('sugo d'oca') is the Umbrian and Veneto version for feast days.
A little dried porcini deepens it.
commonMistakes: Not skimming the fat.
Rushing the braise so the meat won't shred.

recipes.title: Tagliatelle al Ragù Bolognese
recipes.description: Tagliatelle al Ragù Bolognese from Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. A long-simmered meat ragù preparation built on coarsely minced beef chuck, minced pork, pancetta, onion, carrot, celery stalk, dry white wine, passata.

steps.text: Cook the pancetta in a heavy pot until its fat runs. Add the onion, carrot and celery and sweat gently 10 minutes until soft.
Add the beef and pork, breaking them up, and cook over medium heat until no longer pink but not browned hard.
Pour in the wine and simmer until nearly evaporated.
Add the passata, purée, milk and stock. Bring to a bare simmer, part-cover and cook 2.5–3 hours, stirring now and then and topping up with a little stock or water if it dries.
The finished ragù should be thick, glossy and barely soupy. Season.
Cook the tagliatelle in well-salted water, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta with enough ragù to coat generously (not drown), loosening with pasta water. Serve with Parmigiano.

recipes.freezing: Freezes beautifully up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock or milk.
chefTips: The milk keeps the meat tender and takes the edge off the tomato — add it early, not at the end.
A true ragù bolognese is meat-forward with just enough tomato for colour and warmth.
variations: Add 100 g chicken livers with the mince for depth.
Tagliatelle is the Bologna standard; it is never served with spaghetti there.
commonMistakes: Boiling instead of barely simmering — the meat goes dry and grainy.
Too much tomato, turning it into a marinara with mince.

recipes.title: Tortellini in Brodo
recipes.description: Tortellini in Brodo from Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. A filled pasta in clear broth preparation built on fresh tortellini, clear capon or chicken broth, parmigiano-reggiano.

steps.text: Bring the broth to a gentle simmer and check the seasoning.
Slip in the tortellini and cook until they float and the pasta is tender, about 3–4 minutes for fresh.
Ladle into warm bowls with plenty of broth.
Serve with grated Parmigiano at the table.

recipes.storage: Keep pasta and broth separate; combine when serving. 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.freezing: Freeze broth and uncooked pasta separately up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the broth, then cook the pasta in it fresh.
chefTips: The broth must be genuinely good and clear — it is half the dish.
Cook the pasta right in the broth so it seasons the bowl.
variations: 'In brodo' for feast days; the same pasta is served 'asciutti' with butter on other days.
Passatelli (a Parmesan-and-crumb dough pressed through a ricer) is made the same way.
commonMistakes: Boiling the broth hard and clouding it.
Over-filling the bowl with pasta and skimping on broth.

recipes.title: Lasagne Verdi alla Bolognese
recipes.description: Lasagne Verdi alla Bolognese from Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. A layered & baked preparation built on fresh lasagne sheets (spinach), ragù bolognese, béchamel, parmigiano-reggiano, butter.

items.name: béchamel
items.note: 50 g butter, 50 g flour, 800 ml milk, nutmeg

steps.text: Make the béchamel: melt the butter, whisk in the flour and cook 2 minutes, then add warm milk gradually to a pourable sauce. Season with salt, pepper and nutmeg.
Heat the oven to 180°C / 350°F. Butter a baking dish.
Spread a little béchamel on the base. Layer: pasta, ragù, béchamel, Parmigiano. Repeat for 5–6 thin layers.
Finish with béchamel and a generous layer of Parmigiano.
Bake 40–45 minutes until deep golden and bubbling at the edges.
Rest 15 minutes before cutting — this is not optional if you want clean slices.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days; arguably better on day two.
recipes.freezing: Freeze assembled (unbaked) or in cooked portions up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered at 170°C / 340°F for 25–30 minutes.
chefTips: Thin layers, loose sauces — a dry, thickly layered lasagne bakes into a brick.
Bologna uses spinach ('verdi') sheets and no ricotta; ricotta is the southern and Italian-American style.
variations: Lasagne di Carnevale (Naples) adds tiny meatballs, sausage and hard-boiled egg.
A no-boil approach works if the ragù and béchamel are loose enough.
commonMistakes: Too much filling per layer.
Cutting straight away so it slides apart.

recipes.title: Gramigna alla Salsiccia
recipes.description: Gramigna alla Salsiccia from Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. A quick sausage ragù preparation built on fresh gramigna, coarse pork sausage, onion, dry white wine, passata, rosemary, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Soften the onion in the oil. Add the crumbled sausage and brown well.
Add the wine and reduce, then the passata and rosemary. Simmer 25–30 minutes to a thick sauce.
Cook the pasta, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water.
Serve with grated cheese.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: Coarse, fennel-scented sausage makes the best ragù here.
Gnocchetti sardi and gramigna are built to trap this sauce.
variations: A spoon of cream for a Bologna-style gramigna alla salsiccia.
Saffron in the Sardinian (campidanese) version.
commonMistakes: Not browning the sausage.
Cooking the sauce too briefly, leaving it thin and sharp.

recipes.title: Passatelli in Brodo
recipes.description: Passatelli in Brodo from Romagna. A filled pasta in clear broth preparation built on fresh passatelli (parmesan-and-breadcrumb dough pressed through a ricer), clear capon or chicken broth.

items.name: fresh passatelli (Parmesan-and-breadcrumb dough pressed through a ricer)

recipes.title: Garganelli al Prosciutto
recipes.description: Garganelli al Prosciutto from Romagna. A prosciutto & cream preparation built on fresh garganelli, prosciutto or cooked ham, small shallot, double cream, parmigiano-reggiano, butter, peas.

steps.text: Soften the shallot in the butter. Add the prosciutto and warm 1 minute.
Pour in the cream (and peas) and simmer gently to a light sauce.
Cook the pasta, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through with pasta water and the Parmigiano until glossy.
Season with pepper; go easy on salt as the ham is salty.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days; loosen well on reheating.
recipes.freezing: Not recommended.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with extra milk.
chefTips: Add most of the prosciutto at the end so it stays silky, not leathery.
Garganelli and tagliatelle are the Romagna choices.
variations: Add sautéed mushrooms.
A splash of white wine before the cream.
commonMistakes: Boiling the cream hard.
Over-salting.

recipes.title: Maltagliati con Fagioli
recipes.description: Maltagliati con Fagioli from Emilia-Romagna. A pasta & legume soup preparation built on maltagliati, cooked cannellini beans, onion, garlic cloves, celery stalk, tinned tomatoes, rosemary.

items.name: cooked cannellini beans
items.note: with their liquid, or 250 g dried, soaked

steps.text: Sweat the onion, garlic and celery in the oil until soft.
Add the tomatoes, rosemary and Parmigiano rind if using, and cook 5 minutes.
Add the cannellini beans with enough water or stock to cover generously and simmer 20 minutes.
Purée about a third of the soup and stir it back in for body.
Add the pasta and cook until al dente, adding water if it gets too thick.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then serve with a thread of olive oil and pepper.

recipes.storage: Thickens overnight; loosen with water. Keeps 3 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without pasta up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra water or stock, stirring.
chefTips: Blending part of the beans is the trick to a creamy soup without cream.
It should be spoonable but not soupy — 'minestra', not brodo.
variations: Add pancetta or a ham bone for a meatier pot.
Short pasta scraps ('pasta mista') are traditional and stop it feeling like a pasta bowl.
commonMistakes: Cooking the pasta separately and losing the starch that thickens the soup.
Letting it dry out into a stew after resting.

recipes.title: Balanzoni al Burro e Salvia
recipes.description: Balanzoni al Burro e Salvia from Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. A filled pasta in brown butter preparation built on fresh balanzoni (ricotta.

items.name: fresh balanzoni (ricotta, mortadella and herb tortelli)

steps.text: Bring a wide pan of well-salted water to a gentle boil — a hard boil tears filled pasta.
Melt the butter in a large frying pan with the sage and cook until the butter smells nutty and the sage crisps.
Cook the balanzoni (ricotta, mortadella and herb tortelli) 3–4 minutes until they float and the edges are tender.
Lift them straight into the butter with a little pasta water and swirl to emulsify into a glossy sauce.
Serve with Parmigiano and pepper.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the uncooked filled pasta up to 1 month; cook from frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a little butter and water.
chefTips: Keep the water at a gentle simmer so the parcels don't burst.

variations: Brown a few chopped hazelnuts or amaretti in the butter for pumpkin fillings.

commonMistakes: Boiling hard and splitting the pasta.

recipes.title: Pesto alla Genovese con Trofie
recipes.description: Pesto alla Genovese con Trofie from Genoa, Liguria. A raw pounded sauce preparation built on basil leaves, garlic cloves, pine nuts, parmigiano-reggiano, pecorino sardo, mild extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Pound the garlic and a pinch of coarse salt to a paste in a mortar. Add the pine nuts and crush.
Add the basil a little at a time, grinding against the sides with a circular motion until you have a bright green cream.
Work in the cheeses, then trickle in the oil, stirring, until loose and glossy. Do not heat it.
Boil the potatoes 5 minutes, add the green beans for 3 minutes, then add the pasta and cook until al dente.
Loosen the pesto with a spoonful of pasta water in the serving bowl. Drain the pasta and vegetables, toss through, and serve warm — never hot enough to cook the pesto.

recipes.storage: Cover the surface with oil; keeps 3 days refrigerated.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without cheese up to 3 months; stir cheese in after thawing.
recipes.reheating: Do not reheat — dress fresh pasta or serve at room temperature.
chefTips: Keep everything cool. Heat and over-processing turn pesto dark and bitter.
The potatoes and beans are not optional in Liguria — they make the dish.
variations: A blender works if you pulse in short bursts and keep the bowl cold.
Trofie, trenette and mandilli are the classic shapes.
commonMistakes: Blitzing to a hot purée in a food processor.
Tossing into screaming-hot pasta, which greys the sauce.

recipes.title: Trofie al Pesto con Patate e Fagiolini
recipes.description: Trofie al Pesto con Patate e Fagiolini from Liguria. A raw pounded sauce preparation built on basil leaves, garlic cloves, pine nuts, parmigiano-reggiano, pecorino sardo, mild extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Pound the garlic and a pinch of coarse salt to a paste in a mortar. Add the pine nuts and crush.
Add the basil a little at a time, grinding against the sides with a circular motion until you have a bright green cream.
Work in the cheeses, then trickle in the oil, stirring, until loose and glossy. Do not heat it.
Boil the potatoes 5 minutes, add the green beans for 3 minutes, then add the pasta and cook until al dente.
Loosen the pesto with a spoonful of pasta water in the serving bowl. Drain the pasta and vegetables, toss through, and serve warm — never hot enough to cook the pesto.

recipes.storage: Cover the surface with oil; keeps 3 days refrigerated.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without cheese up to 3 months; stir cheese in after thawing.
recipes.reheating: Do not reheat — dress fresh pasta or serve at room temperature.
chefTips: Keep everything cool. Heat and over-processing turn pesto dark and bitter.
The potatoes and beans are not optional in Liguria — they make the dish.
variations: A blender works if you pulse in short bursts and keep the bowl cold.
Trofie, trenette and mandilli are the classic shapes.
commonMistakes: Blitzing to a hot purée in a food processor.
Tossing into screaming-hot pasta, which greys the sauce.

recipes.title: Corzetti al Sugo di Pinoli
recipes.description: Corzetti al Sugo di Pinoli from Liguria. A raw walnut sauce preparation built on shelled walnuts, pine nuts, small garlic clove, stale bread, parmigiano-reggiano, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Blanch the walnuts 1 minute and rub off any loose skins for a sweeter sauce.
Pound or blend the walnuts, pine nuts, garlic, soaked bread and Parmigiano with the oil to a coarse cream.
Loosen with the milk to a pourable sauce. Keep it raw.
Cook the pasta and reserve a little water.
Toss the pasta with the walnut sauce, loosening with pasta water, and serve with a little more Parmigiano.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated with a film of oil on top.
recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Do not cook — dress fresh pasta and loosen with hot water.

The sauce should be thick but pourable; it thickens on standing.

commonMistakes: Skipping the skinning, leaving it bitter.

recipes.title: Testaroli al Pesto
recipes.description: Testaroli al Pesto from Lunigiana, Liguria. A ancient griddle pasta with pesto preparation built on plain flour, water, salt.

steps.text: Whisk the flour, water and salt to a thin, pourable batter and rest 30 minutes.
Cook like thick crêpes in a lightly oiled hot pan — pour a ladle, cover, and cook 2–3 minutes a side until set and lightly spotted.
Cool the testaroli, then cut into large diamonds.
Drop the diamonds into a pot of barely simmering salted water for 1–2 minutes to soften.
Drain gently and toss with pesto loosened with a spoon of the water; serve with grated cheese.

recipes.storage: Cooked testaroli keep 2 days; reheat briefly in warm water.
recipes.freezing: Freeze the cooked, uncut sheets up to 1 month.

Ready-made testaroli just need the brief soak.
commonMistakes: Boiling hard and shredding them.
Cutting the pieces too small.

recipes.title: Spaghetti ai Muscoli
recipes.description: Spaghetti ai Muscoli from La Spezia, Liguria. A sautéed shellfish preparation built on spaghetti, small clams, garlic cloves, dry white wine, extra-virgin olive oil, flat-leaf parsley.

steps.text: Discard any clams that stay open when tapped.
Warm the oil with the garlic (and chilli) for 2 minutes. Add the clams and wine, cover, and cook 3–5 minutes until they open. Discard any that don't.
Lift out most clams and pick the meat, keeping some in shell for serving. Strain the pan juices if gritty and return to the pan.
Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente; drain, reserving water.
Finish the pasta in the clam pan with a little pasta water, tossing hard so the starch emulsifies the juices.
Return all the clams, add the parsley, toss and serve. No cheese.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; shellfish does not keep once dressed.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: Purge the clams well — one gritty clam ruins the plate.
Finishing the pasta in the pan is what makes the sauce cling.
variations: 'In rosso' — add a handful of halved cherry tomatoes with the clams.
A few reserved clam juices whisked with oil off the heat boost the emulsion.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the clams until rubbery.
Adding cheese — never with this sauce.

recipes.title: Taglierini al Limone
recipes.description: Taglierini al Limone from Liguria. A lemon & butter emulsion preparation built on tagliolini, unwaxed lemons, unsalted butter, double cream, parmigiano-reggiano.

items.name: double cream
items.note: or extra pasta water for a lighter version

steps.text: Warm the butter with the lemon zest in a wide pan.
Add the cream (or a ladle of pasta water) and the lemon juice and let it bubble to a light sauce.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the tagliolini. Fresh tagliolini need only 1–2 minutes. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through with pasta water and the Parmigiano until it clings.
Finish with pepper and torn basil or mint.

recipes.storage: Keeps 1 day; the sauce tightens as it cools.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.
chefTips: Zest carries the perfume, juice carries the sharpness — use both, and add juice off the heat so it stays bright.
The Amalfi/Sorrento version leans on sfusato lemons and often skips cream.
variations: Add prawns or courgette ribbons.
A spoon of mascarpone for a silkier sauce.
commonMistakes: Boiling the lemon juice for ages, dulling it.
Too much cream, burying the citrus.

recipes.title: Ravioli di Borragine al Tocco
recipes.description: Ravioli di Borragine al Tocco from Liguria. A filled pasta with a light meat sauce preparation built on braised beef chuck, egg, parmigiano-reggiano, cooked spinach or chard.
recipes.method: Filled pasta with a light meat sauce

items.name: beef chuck ragù or its braising juices
butter
items.note: if dressing with butter instead of ragù

steps.text: Braise the beef chuck until tender, then chop finely and mix with the egg, Parmigiano, greens if using and seasoning into a firm filling.
Make and rest the egg pasta 30 minutes, then roll it very thin.
Fill and shape into borage-and-herb ravioli, sealing each parcel firmly. Keep dusted and covered.
Cook in gently simmering salted water 3–4 minutes until the edges are tender.
Warm the ragù or braising juices (or brown the butter). Lift the pasta in with a little cooking water and turn gently to coat.
Serve with grated Parmigiano.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; refrigerate cooked up to 1 day.
recipes.freezing: Freeze uncooked on a tray, then bag, up to 1 month; cook from frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a little butter or sauce with a splash of water.
chefTips: The filling must be firmly bound and well seasoned — it is the point of the dish.
A gentle simmer, never a rolling boil, or the parcels burst.
variations: Dress simply with sage brown butter and Parmigiano instead of ragù.
A spoon of the braise's reduced juices is often better than a full ragù.
commonMistakes: Loose, wet filling that leaks.
Boiling hard and splitting the pasta.

recipes.title: Orecchiette con Cime di Rapa
recipes.description: Orecchiette con Cime di Rapa from Bari, Puglia. A blanched greens & garlic preparation built on orecchiette, broccoli rabe (cime di rapa), anchovy fillets, garlic cloves, chilli flakes.

steps.text: Blanch the broccoli rabe in salted boiling water 3–4 minutes. Lift it out (keep the water) and roughly chop.
Cook the pasta in the same water.
Melt the anchovies in the oil with the garlic and chilli.
Add the greens and toss well to coat, loosening with a little pasta water.
Drain the pasta a minute early and finish it in the pan with the greens.
Serve with toasted breadcrumbs instead of cheese, Puglia-style.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the dressed greens up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a pan with a splash of water.
chefTips: Cook the pasta in the greens' blanching water for a through-line of flavour.
Orecchiette catches the little florets in its dome.
variations: Add crumbled sausage for a heartier plate.
Swap in purple sprouting broccoli or kale out of season.
commonMistakes: Not blanching long enough, leaving the greens tough and bitter.
Draining the pasta bone dry.

recipes.title: Orecchiette al Sugo di Braciole
recipes.description: Orecchiette al Sugo di Braciole from Puglia. A braised meat ragù preparation built on beef braciole (rolled, onion, garlic cloves, carrot, red wine, crushed tomatoes, bay, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Brown the beef braciole (rolled, stuffed slices) in the oil in batches until well coloured; set aside.
Soften the onion, garlic and carrot in the same pot for 8 minutes.
Return the meat, add the wine and reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes and bay, season, and braise on low heat 1.5–2 hours until the meat is meltingly tender and the sauce is thick.
Cook the orecchiette in well-salted water; reserve a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with grated Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock or water.
chefTips: Brown the beef braciole (rolled, stuffed slices) properly — colour is flavour in a braised ragù.
Keep the heat low and give it time; the meat should shred, not chew.
variations: A strip of orange or lemon peel in the braise lifts gamey meats.
Swap the fresh ribbons for a sturdy tube if that is the local shape.
commonMistakes: Crowding the pan when browning, so the meat steams grey.
Rushing the braise.

recipes.title: Sagne 'ncannulate al Pomodoro
recipes.description: Sagne 'ncannulate al Pomodoro from Salento, Puglia. A simmered tomato preparation built on sagne, ripe tomatoes, garlic cloves, large bunch basil, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Warm the oil with the garlic until fragrant, then discard the garlic.
Add the tomatoes, crushing them, with a few basil leaves and a pinch of salt. Simmer 20–25 minutes until thick and sweet.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the sagne. Twisted sagne cook in 4–6 minutes. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through the sauce with a little pasta water and the rest of the basil, torn.
Finish with olive oil and grated Parmigiano.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the sauce up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently and toss with fresh pasta.
chefTips: A pinch of sugar rounds out sharp out-of-season tomatoes.
Tear the basil in at the end so it stays fragrant.
variations: Stir in a knob of butter at the end for a silkier sauce (Marcella-style).
commonMistakes: Rushing the simmer — the sauce stays watery and raw-tasting.

recipes.title: Cavatelli con Rucola e Cozze
recipes.description: Cavatelli con Rucola e Cozze from Puglia. A sautéed mixed seafood preparation built on cavatelli, clams, mussels, peeled prawns, squid or cuttlefish, garlic cloves, dry white wine.

steps.text: Steam the clams and mussels in the wine in a covered pan until they open, 3–4 minutes. Strain and keep the liquor; shell most of them.
In the same pan, warm the oil and garlic, add the squid and cook 2 minutes, then the prawns for 2 minutes more.
Add the tomatoes if using and the reserved liquor and simmer 5 minutes.
Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente, then finish it in the pan with the seafood and a little pasta water.
Return the shellfish, add parsley, toss and serve. No cheese.

recipes.freezing: Not suitable.

Strain the shellfish liquor — it is the backbone of the sauce, but it can be gritty.
variations: Add a pinch of chilli for 'fra diavolo' heat.
Scoglio (rock) version leaves everything in the shell for drama.
commonMistakes: Boiling the seafood together from cold, so some parts overcook.
Skipping the pan-finish, so the sauce stays thin.

recipes.title: Ciceri e Tria
recipes.description: Ciceri e Tria from Salento, Puglia. A pasta & legume soup preparation built on lagane, cooked chickpeas, onion, garlic cloves, celery stalk, tinned tomatoes, rosemary.

items.name: cooked chickpeas
items.note: with their liquid, or 250 g dried, soaked

steps.text: Sweat the onion, garlic and celery in the oil until soft.
Add the tomatoes, rosemary and Parmigiano rind if using, and cook 5 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with enough water or stock to cover generously and simmer 20 minutes.
Purée about a third of the soup and stir it back in for body.
Add the pasta and cook until al dente, adding water if it gets too thick.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then serve with a thread of olive oil and pepper.

recipes.storage: Thickens overnight; loosen with water. Keeps 3 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without pasta up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra water or stock, stirring.
chefTips: Blending part of the beans is the trick to a creamy soup without cream.
It should be spoonable but not soupy — 'minestra', not brodo.
variations: Add pancetta or a ham bone for a meatier pot.
Short pasta scraps ('pasta mista') are traditional and stop it feeling like a pasta bowl.
commonMistakes: Cooking the pasta separately and losing the starch that thickens the soup.
Letting it dry out into a stew after resting.

recipes.title: Strascinati con Mollica Croccante
recipes.description: Strascinati con Mollica Croccante from Basilicata and Puglia. A sautéed anchovy & crumb preparation built on strascinati, anchovy fillets in oil, garlic cloves, coarse dried breadcrumbs, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Toast the breadcrumbs in 2 tablespoons of the oil until deep gold and crisp; tip onto a plate and salt lightly.
In the same pan warm the rest of the oil with the garlic and chilli, then melt in the anchovies until they dissolve.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the strascinati. Cook 6–9 minutes until springy but firm. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta in the anchovy oil with a splash of pasta water and the parsley.
Serve showered with the toasted crumbs — the 'poor man's Parmesan'.

recipes.storage: Keeps 1 day; add fresh crumbs on reheating.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of water; re-crisp crumbs separately.
chefTips: The crumbs must be properly crisp and golden or they go soggy on the plate.
No cheese — the crumbs are the topping.
variations: Add sultanas and pine nuts for a Sicilian sweet-savoury note.
Wild fennel fronds instead of parsley where you can get them.

Not fully melting the anchovies.

recipes.title: Spaghetti all'Assassina
recipes.description: Spaghetti all'Assassina from Bari, Puglia. A pan-fried 'risottata' preparation built on spaghetti, tins (800 g) tomato passata, garlic cloves, chilli flakes, extra-virgin olive oil, tomato purée.

items.name: tins (800 g) tomato passata
items.note: kept warm and loose with water

steps.text: Make a thin tomato 'brodo': warm the passata with the purée and enough water to make it pourable; keep it hot.
Heat the oil with the garlic and chilli in a wide steel or iron pan until sizzling.
Lay the raw spaghetti in the pan and let it char and stick, turning once, for a minute or two.
Add a ladle of the hot tomato brodo. Let it be absorbed and the pasta catch and char again before adding the next ladle — like a risotto, but you WANT the crust.
Repeat for 12–15 minutes until the spaghetti is cooked, deep red and singed at the edges.
Serve straight from the pan. It is meant to be dark, spicy and a little burnt — that is the point.

recipes.storage: Best straight from the pan; keeps 1 day.
recipes.freezing: Not recommended.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot pan with a splash of tomato water.

commonMistakes: Stirring constantly so it never chars.
Adding all the liquid at once and boiling it soft.

recipes.title: Pasta alla Norma
recipes.description: Pasta alla Norma from Catania, Sicily. A fried aubergine & tomato preparation built on rigatoni, aubergines, tinned tomatoes, garlic cloves, basil, ricotta salata.

items.name: Frying oil, plus 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

steps.text: Salt the aubergine cubes and leave 30 minutes; pat dry.
Fry them in hot oil until deep gold; drain on paper.
Make a quick sauce: soften the garlic in the olive oil, add the tomatoes and a few basil leaves, season and simmer 15 minutes.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the rigatoni. Cook al dente — the ridges must hold the sauce. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta with the tomato sauce, then fold through most of the fried aubergine.
Serve topped with the rest of the aubergine, torn basil and a heavy grating of ricotta salata.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days; keep the aubergine topping separate if you can.
recipes.freezing: Freeze the tomato sauce only.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently; refresh with a little oil.

recipes.title: Anelletti al Forno
recipes.description: Anelletti al Forno from Palermo, Sicily. A baked (al forno) preparation built on anelletti, tomato or meat ragù, fresh mozzarella or fior di latte, parmigiano-reggiano, hard-boiled eggs.

items.name: fresh mozzarella or fior di latte

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C / 400°F. Cook the pasta 3 minutes short of al dente and drain.
Toss the pasta with two-thirds of the ragù.
Layer half in an oiled baking dish with mozzarella, Parmigiano and the optional egg and salami; repeat.
Finish with the remaining ragù and a heavy layer of Parmigiano.
Bake 30–35 minutes until bubbling with a browned, crisp top.
Rest 10–15 minutes before cutting so it holds its shape.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats very well.
recipes.freezing: Freeze cooked portions up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered at 180°C / 350°F for 20 minutes.
chefTips: Undercook the pasta — it keeps cooking in the oven.
Drain the mozzarella well or the bake turns watery.
variations: Anelletti al forno (Palermo) presses the same idea into a tin and turns it out.
A layer of fried aubergine makes it a 'pasta 'ncasciata'.
commonMistakes: Fully cooking the pasta first, so it goes mushy.
Cutting straight from the oven so it collapses.

recipes.title: Pasta con le Sarde
recipes.description: Pasta con le Sarde from Palermo, Sicily. A braised sardine & fennel preparation built on bucatini, fresh sardines, wild fennel, large onion, pine nuts, sultanas, saffron, tomato purée.

steps.text: Boil the fennel in salted water 10 minutes until tender; lift out (keep the water for the pasta) and chop.
Soften the onion in the oil. Add most of the sardines and break them down, then the fennel, saffron water, purée, sultanas and pine nuts. Cook 15 minutes to a soft sauce.
Fry the remaining sardine fillets separately to lay on top.
Cook the pasta in the fennel water, reserving a mugful.
Toss the pasta with the sauce and a little water, top with the reserved fillets and a heavy shower of toasted breadcrumbs.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the sauce base up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently; add fresh breadcrumbs.
chefTips: Pasta con le sarde is sweet-savoury — the sultanas and saffron are meant to be there.
Cook the pasta in the fennel water to carry the flavour through.
variations: 'A mare' (with sardines) for the feast; 'a mari' (without) as an everyday version.
Bucatini is the Palermo choice.
commonMistakes: Skipping the breadcrumbs.
Overcooking the fried fillets until dry.

recipes.title: Busiate al Pesto Trapanese
recipes.description: Busiate al Pesto Trapanese from Trapani, Sicily. A raw blended sauce preparation built on busiate, ripe cherry tomatoes, blanched almonds, garlic clove, large bunch basil, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Blitz or pound the almonds, garlic, basil and a pinch of salt to a coarse paste.
Add the tomatoes and pulse to a rough, chunky sauce, then stir in the oil and Pecorino. Keep it raw.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the busiate. Cook al dente — the coils should keep a firm centre. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the hot pasta with the pesto, loosening with pasta water.
Serve with extra Pecorino and torn basil.

recipes.freezing: Not recommended — raw tomato weeps.
recipes.reheating: Serve at room temperature; do not cook the sauce.
chefTips: Trapani's version uses almonds, not pine nuts, and raw tomato — it is a summer sauce.
Busiate, the local coiled shape, catches it perfectly.
variations: Add a little tomato passata if the fresh tomatoes are pale.
commonMistakes: Over-blending to a smooth purée — it should have texture.

recipes.title: Maccheroni al Sugo di Maiale
recipes.description: Maccheroni al Sugo di Maiale from Sicily. A braised meat ragù preparation built on pork ribs and shoulder, onion, garlic cloves, carrot, red wine, crushed tomatoes, bay and chilli.

steps.text: Brown the pork ribs and shoulder in the oil in batches until well coloured; set aside.
Soften the onion, garlic and carrot in the same pot for 8 minutes.
Return the meat, add the wine and reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes and bay and chilli, season, and braise on low heat 1.5–2 hours until the meat is meltingly tender and the sauce is thick.
Cook the maccheroni in well-salted water; reserve a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with grated Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock or water.
chefTips: Brown the pork ribs and shoulder properly — colour is flavour in a braised ragù.
Keep the heat low and give it time; the meat should shred, not chew.
variations: A strip of orange or lemon peel in the braise lifts gamey meats.
Swap the fresh ribbons for a sturdy tube if that is the local shape.
commonMistakes: Crowding the pan when browning, so the meat steams grey.
Rushing the braise.

recipes.title: Cavatelli con Broccoli Arriminati
recipes.description: Cavatelli con Broccoli Arriminati from Sicily. A braised cauliflower preparation built on cavatelli, cauliflower, onion, sultanas, pine nuts, anchovy fillets, saffron, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Boil the cauliflower in salted water until just tender; scoop out (keep the water) and set aside.
Soften the onion in the oil, melt in the anchovies, then add the sultanas, pine nuts and saffron water.
Add the cauliflower and crush it lightly so some breaks down into a sauce. Loosen with cauliflower water.
Cook the pasta in the cauliflower water; drain and toss through the pan.
Serve with toasted breadcrumbs.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: 'Arriminata' means stirred/mashed — you want half sauce, half florets.
The saffron and sultanas make it unmistakably Palermitano.
variations: Add a little tomato purée for a rosy version.
commonMistakes: Leaving the cauliflower in big firm lumps with no sauce.

recipes.title: Spaghetti ai Ricci di Mare
recipes.description: Spaghetti ai Ricci di Mare from Sicily. A raw sea-urchin finish preparation built on spaghetti, sea urchin roe, garlic cloves, extra-virgin olive oil, chilli flakes, small handful parsley.

items.name: sea urchin roe
items.note: from about 40 urchins, or a good jar

steps.text: Warm the oil with the garlic and chilli; discard the garlic. Take off the heat.
Cook the pasta, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the drained pasta in the warm oil with a little pasta water.
Off the heat, fold through most of the urchin roe so it melts into a sauce without cooking.
Plate and top each portion with a few whole tongues of roe. No cheese.

recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: The roe must not cook — fold it in off the heat at the very end.
Balance is everything: too much and it turns bitter-metallic.
variations: A little lemon zest.
Some cooks add a spoon of tomato passata.
commonMistakes: Adding the roe to a hot pan.
Overloading the dish with roe.

recipes.title: Timballo di Anelletti
recipes.description: Timballo di Anelletti from Sicily. A baked (al forno) preparation built on anelletti, tomato or meat ragù, fresh mozzarella or fior di latte, parmigiano-reggiano, hard-boiled eggs.

items.name: fresh mozzarella or fior di latte

steps.text: Heat the oven to 200°C / 400°F. Cook the pasta 3 minutes short of al dente and drain.
Toss the pasta with two-thirds of the ragù.
Layer half in an oiled baking dish with mozzarella, Parmigiano and the optional egg and salami; repeat.
Finish with the remaining ragù and a heavy layer of Parmigiano.
Bake 30–35 minutes until bubbling with a browned, crisp top.
Rest 10–15 minutes before cutting so it holds its shape.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and reheats very well.
recipes.freezing: Freeze cooked portions up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat covered at 180°C / 350°F for 20 minutes.
chefTips: Undercook the pasta — it keeps cooking in the oven.
Drain the mozzarella well or the bake turns watery.
variations: Anelletti al forno (Palermo) presses the same idea into a tin and turns it out.
A layer of fried aubergine makes it a 'pasta 'ncasciata'.
commonMistakes: Fully cooking the pasta first, so it goes mushy.
Cutting straight from the oven so it collapses.

recipes.title: Casarecce alla Siciliana
recipes.description: Casarecce alla Siciliana from Sicily. A fried aubergine & tomato preparation built on casarecce, aubergines, tinned tomatoes, garlic cloves, basil, ricotta salata.

items.name: Frying oil, plus 3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

steps.text: Salt the aubergine cubes and leave 30 minutes; pat dry.
Fry them in hot oil until deep gold; drain on paper.
Make a quick sauce: soften the garlic in the olive oil, add the tomatoes and a few basil leaves, season and simmer 15 minutes.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the casarecce. Cook al dente, about 1 minute under the packet. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta with the tomato sauce, then fold through most of the fried aubergine.
Serve topped with the rest of the aubergine, torn basil and a heavy grating of ricotta salata.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days; keep the aubergine topping separate if you can.
recipes.freezing: Freeze the tomato sauce only.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently; refresh with a little oil.
chefTips: Salting and properly frying the aubergine (not baking) is what makes it Norma.
Ricotta salata, not Parmesan — it is salty and firm, like a mild feta.
variations: Bake the aubergine in plenty of oil if you prefer, but fried is classic.
Rigatoni or spaghetti both work.
commonMistakes: Skipping the salting step, so the aubergine soaks up oil.
Using soft fresh ricotta instead of ricotta salata.

recipes.title: Pasta con Tenerumi
recipes.description: Pasta con Tenerumi from Palermo, Sicily. A vegetable & pasta soup preparation built on small pasta or broken spaghetti, borlotti or cannellini beans, onion, potato, seasonal vegetables.

steps.text: Sweat the onion, carrot and celery in the oil 10 minutes.
Add the potato, tomatoes and Parmigiano rind and cover with water or light stock. Simmer 20 minutes.
Add the rest of the vegetables and the beans and simmer 20 minutes more until everything is tender; mash a little for body.
Add the pasta and cook until al dente, loosening with water as needed.
Rest 10 minutes off the heat. Serve with a spoon of pesto (Genoese-style) or grated Parmigiano and olive oil.

recipes.freezing: Freeze without pasta up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra water or stock.
chefTips: Minestrone is better after resting — make it ahead.
A Parmigiano rind simmered in gives savoury depth for free.
variations: Genoese minestrone finishes with a spoon of pesto.
Rice instead of pasta in parts of Lombardy and Veneto.
commonMistakes: Cooking the pasta separately and losing the starch.
Serving it piping hot straight off the heat — it wants to settle.

recipes.title: Spaghetti alle Vongole
recipes.description: Spaghetti alle Vongole from Naples, Campania. A sautéed shellfish preparation built on spaghetti, small clams, garlic cloves, dry white wine, extra-virgin olive oil, flat-leaf parsley.

steps.text: Discard any clams that stay open when tapped.
Warm the oil with the garlic (and chilli) for 2 minutes. Add the clams and wine, cover, and cook 3–5 minutes until they open. Discard any that don't.
Lift out most clams and pick the meat, keeping some in shell for serving. Strain the pan juices if gritty and return to the pan.
Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente; drain, reserving water.
Finish the pasta in the clam pan with a little pasta water, tossing hard so the starch emulsifies the juices.
Return all the clams, add the parsley, toss and serve. No cheese.

recipes.storage: Eat immediately; shellfish does not keep once dressed.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: Purge the clams well — one gritty clam ruins the plate.
Finishing the pasta in the pan is what makes the sauce cling.
variations: 'In rosso' — add a handful of halved cherry tomatoes with the clams.
A few reserved clam juices whisked with oil off the heat boost the emulsion.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the clams until rubbery.
Adding cheese — never with this sauce.

recipes.title: Pasta e Patate con Provola
recipes.description: Pasta e Patate con Provola from Naples, Campania. A one-pot pasta & potato preparation built on pasta mista, potatoes, onion, celery stalk, pancetta, tomato purée, parmigiano rind.

steps.text: Sweat the onion, celery and pancetta in the oil until soft.
Add the potatoes, purée and Parmigiano rind, then just enough water to cover. Simmer 15 minutes until the potatoes start to break down.
Add the pasta and cook in the same pot, stirring, adding hot water as needed to keep it loose.
When the pasta is al dente the dish should be creamy from the potato starch.
Off the heat, stir through the diced provola so it turns stringy, and rest 2 minutes before serving.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days; loosen with water on reheating.
recipes.freezing: Not recommended — potato texture suffers.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: Cook the pasta right in the potato pot — the released starch is the sauce.
The 'azzeccata' (sticky, almost burnt bottom) is prized in Naples.
variations: Leave out the provola for a lighter version.
A crushed dried chilli is welcome.
commonMistakes: Adding too much water and ending up with soup.
Under-cooking the potatoes so they don't thicken the dish.

recipes.title: Ziti alla Genovese
recipes.description: Ziti alla Genovese from Naples, Campania. A slow onion & beef braise preparation built on white or golden onions, beef chuck or shin, carrot, celery stalk, dry white wine, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Brown the beef in the oil in a heavy pot; add the wine and let it reduce.
Pile in the onions, carrot and celery — it will look like far too much onion. Add a splash of water, cover, and cook on the lowest heat.
Cook 3–3.5 hours, stirring now and then, until the onions completely collapse into a sweet, deep-brown sauce and the beef is falling apart.
Uncover for the last 30 minutes to concentrate. Season.
Cook the pasta, reserving a mugful of water, and toss with the sauce and a little pasta water.
Serve with mixed Parmigiano and Pecorino. The beef follows as a second course.

recipes.storage: Better the next day; keeps 4 days refrigerated.
recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: No tomato — the colour and sweetness come entirely from the onions cooking down for hours.
Ziti snapped by hand, rigatoni or paccheri are the Naples shapes.
variations: A little pancetta or salami in the base deepens it.
Some families add a splash of vinegar at the end for lift.
commonMistakes: Rushing the onions on high heat so they fry instead of melting.
Not using enough onion — the ratio really is about 2:1 onion to meat.

recipes.title: Paccheri al Ragù Napoletano
recipes.description: Paccheri al Ragù Napoletano from Naples, Campania. A sunday meat ragù preparation built on beef short rib or chuck, pork ribs or sausage, large onion, red wine, tins (800 g) crushed tomatoes.

steps.text: Brown the meat well in the oil in a heavy pot, in batches; set aside.
Lower the heat, add the onion and cook slowly 10 minutes until soft and golden.
Return the meat, add the wine and let it reduce.
Stir in the purée, then the tomatoes and basil. Bring to the barest simmer.
Cook uncovered on the lowest heat 3–3.5 hours, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is dark red and the meat is falling apart. Season.
Lift out the meat to serve as a second course. Toss the cooked pasta with the sauce and a little pasta water.
Serve with grated cheese; the meat follows.

recipes.storage: Better the next day; keeps 4 days refrigerated.
recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: Neapolitan ragù is about the long, slow 'pippiare' — the sauce should barely blip for hours.
The meat is traditionally eaten after the pasta, not with it.
variations: Add braciole (rolled, stuffed beef) to the pot.
Paccheri, ziti snapped by hand, or rigatoni are all classic.
commonMistakes: Cooking too fast, so the meat toughens before the sauce sweetens.
Skimping on browning, which costs you the deep flavour.

recipes.title: Pasta e Fagioli alla Napoletana
recipes.description: Pasta e Fagioli alla Napoletana from Naples, Campania. A pasta & legume soup preparation built on pasta mista, cooked borlotti beans, onion, garlic cloves, celery stalk, tinned tomatoes, rosemary.

items.name: cooked borlotti beans
items.note: with their liquid, or 250 g dried, soaked

steps.text: Sweat the onion, garlic and celery in the oil until soft.
Add the tomatoes, rosemary and Parmigiano rind if using, and cook 5 minutes.
Add the borlotti beans with enough water or stock to cover generously and simmer 20 minutes.
Purée about a third of the soup and stir it back in for body.
Add the pasta and cook until al dente, adding water if it gets too thick.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then serve with a thread of olive oil and pepper.

recipes.storage: Thickens overnight; loosen with water. Keeps 3 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without pasta up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra water or stock, stirring.
chefTips: Blending part of the beans is the trick to a creamy soup without cream.
It should be spoonable but not soupy — 'minestra', not brodo.
variations: Add pancetta or a ham bone for a meatier pot.
Short pasta scraps ('pasta mista') are traditional and stop it feeling like a pasta bowl.
commonMistakes: Cooking the pasta separately and losing the starch that thickens the soup.
Letting it dry out into a stew after resting.

recipes.title: Spaghetti alla Nerano
recipes.description: Spaghetti alla Nerano from Sorrento, Campania. A fried courgette & cheese preparation built on spaghetti, courgettes, provolone del monaco, parmigiano-reggiano, basil.

items.name: Frying oil, plus 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil

steps.text: Fry the courgette rounds in batches in hot oil until golden; drain on paper and salt lightly. Do this ahead if you can — some rest improves them.
Cook the pasta, reserving two mugs of water.
In a wide pan, warm the olive oil, add most of the fried courgettes and a ladle of pasta water and crush some to a rough sauce.
Add the drained pasta, the cheeses and more pasta water, and toss hard off the heat until creamy and stringy.
Fold through the basil and the reserved courgettes and serve at once.

recipes.freezing: Not recommended.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with plenty of added water.
chefTips: Frying (not steaming) the courgettes and letting them rest is the soul of Nerano.
Toss vigorously off the heat so the Provolone melts into a cream, not a lump.
variations: A little butter helps the emulsion.
Spaghetti or linguine are the Nerano shapes.
commonMistakes: Skipping the fry.
Adding the cheese over high heat so it seizes.

recipes.title: Linguine al Limone di Sorrento
recipes.description: Linguine al Limone di Sorrento from Campania. A lemon & butter emulsion preparation built on linguine, unwaxed lemons, unsalted butter, double cream, parmigiano-reggiano.

items.name: double cream
items.note: or extra pasta water for a lighter version

steps.text: Warm the butter with the lemon zest in a wide pan.
Add the cream (or a ladle of pasta water) and the lemon juice and let it bubble to a light sauce.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the linguine. Cook until al dente, keeping a little bite. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through with pasta water and the Parmigiano until it clings.
Finish with pepper and torn basil or mint.

recipes.storage: Keeps 1 day; the sauce tightens as it cools.
recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water and a fresh squeeze of lemon.
chefTips: Zest carries the perfume, juice carries the sharpness — use both, and add juice off the heat so it stays bright.
The Amalfi/Sorrento version leans on sfusato lemons and often skips cream.
variations: Add prawns or courgette ribbons.
A spoon of mascarpone for a silkier sauce.
commonMistakes: Boiling the lemon juice for ages, dulling it.
Too much cream, burying the citrus.

recipes.title: Scialatielli ai Frutti di Mare
recipes.description: Scialatielli ai Frutti di Mare from Amalfi Coast, Campania. A sautéed mixed seafood preparation built on scialatielli, clams, mussels, peeled prawns, squid or cuttlefish, garlic cloves, dry white wine.

steps.text: Steam the clams and mussels in the wine in a covered pan until they open, 3–4 minutes. Strain and keep the liquor; shell most of them.
In the same pan, warm the oil and garlic, add the squid and cook 2 minutes, then the prawns for 2 minutes more.
Add the tomatoes if using and the reserved liquor and simmer 5 minutes.
Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente, then finish it in the pan with the seafood and a little pasta water.
Return the shellfish, add parsley, toss and serve. No cheese.

recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: Cook each seafood only until just done, then bring it all together at the end.
Strain the shellfish liquor — it is the backbone of the sauce, but it can be gritty.
variations: Add a pinch of chilli for 'fra diavolo' heat.
Scoglio (rock) version leaves everything in the shell for drama.
commonMistakes: Boiling the seafood together from cold, so some parts overcook.
Skipping the pan-finish, so the sauce stays thin.

recipes.title: Mezzi Paccheri con Pesce Spada
recipes.description: Mezzi Paccheri con Pesce Spada from Campania. A sautéed swordfish preparation built on mezzi paccheri, swordfish, cherry tomatoes, garlic cloves, pitted green olives, capers, small aubergine.

steps.text: Sear the swordfish dice briefly in hot oil until just coloured; lift out.
Soften the garlic in the pan, add the tomatoes, olives and capers and cook 8–10 minutes to a loose sauce.
Return the swordfish (and fried aubergine if using) and warm through — it should stay just cooked.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the mezzi paccheri. Cook al dente with a firm rim. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through with a little pasta water and the herbs.

recipes.storage: Keeps 1 day; fish texture suffers after that.
recipes.freezing: Not recommended.
recipes.reheating: Reheat very gently.
chefTips: Swordfish dries out fast — sear, remove, and return it only to warm through.
Mint is the Sicilian herb of choice here.
variations: Add a pinch of cinnamon or a few pine nuts for a Messina 'a ghiotta' note.
commonMistakes: Overcooking the fish.
Letting the sauce reduce too far and go jammy.

recipes.title: Pasta e Ceci con Rosmarino
recipes.description: Pasta e Ceci con Rosmarino from Campania. A pasta & legume soup preparation built on pasta mista, cooked chickpeas, onion, garlic cloves, celery stalk, tinned tomatoes, rosemary.

items.name: cooked chickpeas
items.note: with their liquid, or 250 g dried, soaked

steps.text: Sweat the onion, garlic and celery in the oil until soft.
Add the tomatoes, rosemary and Parmigiano rind if using, and cook 5 minutes.
Add the chickpeas with enough water or stock to cover generously and simmer 20 minutes.
Purée about a third of the soup and stir it back in for body.
Add the pasta and cook until al dente, adding water if it gets too thick.
Rest 5 minutes off the heat, then serve with a thread of olive oil and pepper.

recipes.storage: Thickens overnight; loosen with water. Keeps 3 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze without pasta up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra water or stock, stirring.
chefTips: Blending part of the beans is the trick to a creamy soup without cream.
It should be spoonable but not soupy — 'minestra', not brodo.
variations: Add pancetta or a ham bone for a meatier pot.
Short pasta scraps ('pasta mista') are traditional and stop it feeling like a pasta bowl.
commonMistakes: Cooking the pasta separately and losing the starch that thickens the soup.
Letting it dry out into a stew after resting.

recipes.title: Pici all'Aglione
recipes.description: Pici all'Aglione from Tuscany. A garlic & tomato with hand-rolled pici preparation built on '00' or bread flour, warm water, olive oil, salt.

items.name: large garlic cloves
items.note: aglione if you can get it, sliced

steps.text: Make a firm dough with the pici ingredients, knead 10 minutes, and rest 30 minutes covered.
Roll pieces into thick, uneven spaghetti-like strands with your palms — pici are meant to be rustic.
For the sauce, warm the sliced garlic very gently in the oil until soft and sweet, not coloured, then add the tomatoes and chilli and simmer 20 minutes.
Cook the pici in well-salted water 4–6 minutes until springy; reserve water.
Toss the pici through the sauce with a little pasta water. Serve with grated Pecorino Toscano.

recipes.storage: Sauce keeps 4 days; fresh pici keep 1 day or freeze.
recipes.freezing: Freeze fresh pici on a tray, then bag, up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce and cook fresh pici to serve.
chefTips: Aglione is a giant, mellow garlic — regular garlic works, just cook it low and slow so it turns sweet.
Pici want a firm dough and no egg; the chew is the point.
variations: Pici all'aglione, cacio e pepe, or with a duck ragù are the Val di Chiana classics.
Dried pici from a packet cut the work.
commonMistakes: Browning the garlic, which turns it bitter.
Rolling the pici too thin.

recipes.title: Pappardelle al Cinghiale
recipes.description: Pappardelle al Cinghiale from Tuscany. A braised meat ragù preparation built on wild boar shoulder, onion, garlic cloves, carrot, red wine, crushed tomatoes, juniper and rosemary.

steps.text: Brown the wild boar shoulder in the oil in batches until well coloured; set aside.
Soften the onion, garlic and carrot in the same pot for 8 minutes.
Return the meat, add the wine and reduce by half.
Add the tomatoes and juniper and rosemary, season, and braise on low heat 1.5–2 hours until the meat is meltingly tender and the sauce is thick.
Cook the pappardelle in well-salted water; reserve a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with grated Pecorino.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock or water.
chefTips: Brown the wild boar shoulder properly — colour is flavour in a braised ragù.
Keep the heat low and give it time; the meat should shred, not chew.
variations: A strip of orange or lemon peel in the braise lifts gamey meats.
Swap the fresh ribbons for a sturdy tube if that is the local shape.
commonMistakes: Crowding the pan when browning, so the meat steams grey.
Rushing the braise.

recipes.title: Ribollita con Pane e Cavolo Nero
recipes.description: Ribollita con Pane e Cavolo Nero from Tuscany. A twice-cooked bread & bean soup preparation built on stale tuscan bread, cannellini beans, cavolo nero, savoy cabbage and chard, onion, tinned tomatoes.

steps.text: Sweat the onion, carrot, celery and garlic in the oil 12 minutes.
Add the tomatoes, the puréed and whole beans, and the greens with enough water to cover. Simmer 45 minutes until thick.
Stir in the torn bread and simmer 15 minutes more until it collapses into the soup.
Cool and rest — ideally overnight.
The next day, reheat gently ('ribollita' means reboiled), adjusting with water, and serve with a generous thread of new olive oil and pepper.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a little water; finish with raw oil.
chefTips: Ribollita is deliberately made a day ahead and reheated — that second cooking is the dish.
It should be thick enough to stand a spoon in, not soupy.
variations: A crushed dried chilli and a rubbed garlic clove on toasted bread underneath.
Some add a little cavolo nero raw at the end for colour.
commonMistakes: Serving it the same day, thin and bready.
Skimping on the finishing oil.

recipes.title: Pici al Ragù d'Anatra
recipes.description: Pici al Ragù d'Anatra from Tuscany. A slow poultry ragù preparation built on duck legs, onion, garlic cloves, red wine, crushed tomatoes, rosemary and a bay leaf, extra-virgin olive oil.

items.name: sprig rosemary and a bay leaf

steps.text: Brown the duck legs well in the oil, skin-side first, rendering the fat; set aside and pour off most of the fat.
Soften the soffritto and garlic in the pan 10 minutes.
Return the duck legs, add the wine and reduce, then the tomatoes and herbs. Braise gently 2 hours until the meat falls from the bone.
Lift out the bones, shred the meat and return it; reduce to a thick ragù. Season.
Cook the pici and toss through the ragù with a little pasta water. Serve with Parmigiano.

recipes.storage: Better the next day; keeps 4 days.
recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of stock.
chefTips: Render the duck legs skin properly — that fat carries the flavour of the whole sauce.
Skim excess fat before serving; poultry ragù can be rich.
variations: Goose ('sugo d'oca') is the Umbrian and Veneto version for feast days.
A little dried porcini deepens it.
commonMistakes: Not skimming the fat.
Rushing the braise so the meat won't shred.

recipes.title: Tagliatelle ai Funghi Porcini

recipes.title: Risi e Bisi
recipes.description: Risi e Bisi from Venice, Veneto. A loose rice & pea 'minestra' preparation built on vialone nano rice, fresh peas, small onion, pancetta, light stock, butter, parmigiano-reggiano, parsley.

recipes.title: Ravioli del Plin al Burro
recipes.description: Ravioli del Plin al Burro from Piedmont. A filled pasta in brown butter preparation built on fresh plin (tiny roast-meat ravioli).

steps.text: Bring a wide pan of well-salted water to a gentle boil — a hard boil tears filled pasta.
Melt the butter in a large frying pan with the sage and cook until the butter smells nutty and the sage crisps.
Cook the plin (tiny roast-meat ravioli) 3–4 minutes until they float and the edges are tender.
Lift them straight into the butter with a little pasta water and swirl to emulsify into a glossy sauce.
Serve with Parmigiano and pepper.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the uncooked filled pasta up to 1 month; cook from frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a little butter and water.
chefTips: Keep the water at a gentle simmer so the parcels don't burst.
A spoon of pasta water in the butter turns it from greasy to silky.
variations: Brown a few chopped hazelnuts or amaretti in the butter for pumpkin fillings.
A whisper of nutmeg suits ricotta fillings.
commonMistakes: Boiling hard and splitting the pasta.
Letting the butter burn past nut-brown to black.

recipes.title: Agnolotti al Brasato
recipes.description: Agnolotti al Brasato from Piedmont. A filled pasta with a light meat sauce preparation built on braised braised beef (brasato al barolo), egg, parmigiano-reggiano, cooked spinach or chard.
recipes.method: Filled pasta with a light meat sauce

items.name: braised beef (brasato al Barolo) ragù or its braising juices
butter
items.note: if dressing with butter instead of ragù

steps.text: Braise the braised beef (brasato al Barolo) until tender, then chop finely and mix with the egg, Parmigiano, greens if using and seasoning into a firm filling.
Make and rest the egg pasta 30 minutes, then roll it very thin.
Fill and shape into agnolotti, sealing each parcel firmly. Keep dusted and covered.
Cook in gently simmering salted water 3–4 minutes until the edges are tender.
Warm the ragù or braising juices (or brown the butter). Lift the pasta in with a little cooking water and turn gently to coat.
Serve with grated Parmigiano.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; refrigerate cooked up to 1 day.
recipes.freezing: Freeze uncooked on a tray, then bag, up to 1 month; cook from frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a little butter or sauce with a splash of water.
chefTips: The filling must be firmly bound and well seasoned — it is the point of the dish.
A gentle simmer, never a rolling boil, or the parcels burst.
variations: Dress simply with sage brown butter and Parmigiano instead of ragù.
A spoon of the braise's reduced juices is often better than a full ragù.
commonMistakes: Loose, wet filling that leaks.
Boiling hard and splitting the pasta.

recipes.title: Risotto al Barolo
recipes.description: Risotto al Barolo from Piedmont. A risotto (mantecato) preparation built on carnaroli or arborio rice, small onion, hot light stock, dry white wine, extra-virgin olive oil or butter.

steps.text: Sweat the onion in the fat until soft and translucent, without colour.
Add the rice and toast 2 minutes until the grains are hot and slightly translucent at the edges.
Pour in the wine and stir until absorbed.
Add hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often, waiting until each addition is nearly absorbed before the next. This takes 16–18 minutes; the rice should stay al dente.
Beat in cold butter and Parmigiano off the heat until glossy (the 'mantecatura').
Rest 2 minutes, then serve 'all'onda' — loose enough to ripple on the plate.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 1 month; best repurposed as arancini.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with extra stock, stirring, or fry as cakes.
chefTips: Keep the stock hot — cold stock stalls the cook and makes it gluey.
The 'mantecatura' (beating in cold fat off the heat) is what makes it creamy, not cream.
variations: Leftover risotto sets and fries into 'risotto al salto' or arancini.
A spoon of bone marrow is the old Milanese touch.
commonMistakes: Adding all the stock at once.
Cooking the rice to mush — stop while it has bite.

recipes.title: Maccheroni al Ferretto
recipes.description: Maccheroni al Ferretto from Piedmont. A quick sausage ragù preparation built on fresh maccheroni, coarse pork sausage, onion, dry white wine, passata, rosemary, extra-virgin olive oil.

steps.text: Soften the onion in the oil. Add the crumbled sausage and brown well.
Add the wine and reduce, then the passata and rosemary. Simmer 25–30 minutes to a thick sauce.
Cook the pasta, reserving a mugful of water.
Toss the pasta through the ragù with a little pasta water.
Serve with grated cheese.

recipes.freezing: Freeze up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water.
chefTips: Coarse, fennel-scented sausage makes the best ragù here.
Gnocchetti sardi and gramigna are built to trap this sauce.
variations: A spoon of cream for a Bologna-style gramigna alla salsiccia.
Saffron in the Sardinian (campidanese) version.
commonMistakes: Not browning the sausage.
Cooking the sauce too briefly, leaving it thin and sharp.

recipes.title: Tagliolini ai Funghi
recipes.description: Tagliolini ai Funghi from Piedmont. A sautéed mushrooms preparation built on fresh tagliolini, mixed mushrooms, garlic cloves, dry white wine, small handful parsley.

items.name: mixed mushrooms
items.note: or 400 g porcini (30 g dried + fresh)

steps.text: If using dried porcini, soak in warm water 20 minutes; keep the strained liquor.
Sear the mushrooms in hot oil in a wide pan without crowding, until browned. Add the garlic for the last minute.
Add the wine (and porcini liquor) and simmer until nearly gone.
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a rolling boil and cook the tagliolini. Fresh tagliolini need only 1–2 minutes. Reserve a mugful of pasta water before draining.
Toss the pasta through with a little pasta water and the parsley.
Serve with grated Parmigiano.

recipes.freezing: Freeze the mushroom sauce up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a pan with a splash of water.
chefTips: Get real colour on the mushrooms — pale, steamed mushrooms taste of nothing.
A little dried porcini deepens even a plain-mushroom sauce.
variations: Finish with a spoon of cream or mascarpone for a northern version.
A little sausage meat turns it into a heartier ragù.
commonMistakes: Crowding the pan so the mushrooms stew.
Under-seasoning — mushrooms need salt.

recipes.title: Fregola con Arselle
recipes.description: Fregola con Arselle from Sardinia. A sautéed mixed seafood preparation built on fregola, clams, mussels, peeled prawns, squid or cuttlefish, garlic cloves, dry white wine, cherry tomatoes.

steps.text: Steam the clams and mussels in the wine in a covered pan until they open, 3–4 minutes. Strain and keep the liquor; shell most of them.
In the same pan, warm the oil and garlic, add the squid and cook 2 minutes, then the prawns for 2 minutes more.
Add the tomatoes if using and the reserved liquor and simmer 5 minutes.
Cook the pasta 2 minutes short of al dente, then finish it in the pan with the seafood and a little pasta water.
Return the shellfish, add parsley, toss and serve. No cheese.

recipes.freezing: Not suitable.
recipes.reheating: Not recommended.
chefTips: Cook each seafood only until just done, then bring it all together at the end.
Strain the shellfish liquor — it is the backbone of the sauce, but it can be gritty.
variations: Add a pinch of chilli for 'fra diavolo' heat.
Scoglio (rock) version leaves everything in the shell for drama.
commonMistakes: Boiling the seafood together from cold, so some parts overcook.
Skipping the pan-finish, so the sauce stays thin.
